This is the signature week of the course: the same research question answered by **both** of statistics' great traditions, side by side — the reason we use the Stanton book at all. Session 5's confidence intervals grow into the Null Hypothesis Significance Test (fine print included), and then Session 3's Bayes' theorem returns — pointed at hypotheses instead of diagnoses, answering the question you probably *meant* to ask. Every method from here to the end of the course runs in both traditions, so this week's vocabulary is permanent.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this week you can:

- run `t.test()` *and* `ttestBF()` on the same question, and state correctly what each output licenses you to claim
- explain in plain language what a p-value is — and name the things it is not
- read a Bayes factor and a posterior distribution, and report a credible interval honestly
- join related tables with `left_join()`, `inner_join()`, and `anti_join()`, checking keys and missing values first

## Before class

- Read: Stanton **Ch. 5** (Bayesian & Frequentist Hypothesis Testing)
- Read: Mourtgos, S. M. (2023). "Bayesian Inference in Criminological Research." *Police Forum*, 32(1), 7–16 — PDF posted on Canvas. Yes, I assigned my own article; consider it a preview of where your instructor's sympathies lie, and feel free to argue with it in class
- Read: R4DS **[Ch. 19 — Joins](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/joins.html)**; skim **[Ch. 18 — Missing values](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/missing-values.html)** — **plus the exercises assigned in [Session 5](week-05.qmd#homework)**
- Install the Bayesian engine before class so we can use it together: `install.packages("BayesFactor")`

## In class

**This week's two threads:** hypothesis testing in both traditions (lecture + homework) · joins (lab).

- From Session 5's confidence intervals to the **Null Hypothesis Significance Test**: bootstrap logic, the null, the verdict machine — and an animation of what the p-value is actually doing
- What a p-value is, and the long list of things it is not
- The fine print: NHST never scores the alternative hypothesis, and rarely checks the distribution it assumes
- **Bayes' theorem, recapped from Session 3** — and the new insight: the p-value lives entirely in the likelihood, and never becomes P(H₀ | data); the two traditions side by side
- Optional self-study appendix (end of the deck): why Bayes was long impractical (the intractable denominator) and how **MCMC** solved it, watched live
- Both traditions on our real Chicago question — `t.test()` says *significant*, `ttestBF()` mildly favors the null, the posterior says the difference is almost surely real *and* almost surely trivial. Sorting out that collision (effect sizes!) is the heart of the week
- The recidivism trial: p = 0.20 vs. a 91% posterior probability the program works — same data, different questions
- Sample size pathologies, animated: p-values dive below .05 for trivial effects as *n* grows; posteriors just sharpen around the truth
- **Lab 6:** joining the two Chicago files — `left_join()`, `inner_join()`, `anti_join()`, key checks, and the missing-values discipline ([lab page](../labs/lab-06-joins.qmd))
